This happened a few weeks ago when I was on my 15 minute break from work. I live very close to the office, so I walk home, use the restroom (thank god for proximity so I don't have to poop at work), and have a quick lunch. There's a gas station between my home and work, so I stop in there to grab a snack for later in the afternoon. There's one person at the register, so I get in line behind them. Then a college-aged kid gets in line behind me, and a guy dressed in a blue camo BDU carrying a fountain drink steps up next to us. The college kid behind me offers to let the soldier go ahead, and he replies, "oh I'm not in line." The customer in front of me leaves and I step up to the register, and the cashier explains why he's not in line. "Nope, we don't make him pay for his drinks. He's served our country." The kid who initially offered smiles and mentions again that he wouldn't make a soldier wait in line. The cashier says, "well that's sweet of you," while giving me a bit of a glare, I assume for not offering my own spot in line. I pay and grab my items, and as I'm walking out I hear the soldier say, "I wish all the [name of franchise]s down in [city 30 miles south] had the same appreciation! They always make me pay for drinks."

It wasn't anything overly obscene, but the whole interaction just left me feeling... slimy, like I had been covered in their self-congratulatory jizz. Since then I've felt myself trying to avoid going in there, although I still do sometimes. The cashier is great with faces, and she definitely recognizes me. I know one of my coworkers also stops in there frequently and knows this female cashier, but I don't want to bring it up with her because I can already imagine the, "Yeah, you're an asshole for being bothered by that" response I would get. Very glad I can come here and vent about it.

Say we are talking about the Breast Cancer (BrCa) gene. While women without the gene have a 12% chance of getting breast cancer in their lifetimes, women who have that a harmful BrCa 1 mutation have about a 50:50 shot of getting breast cancer in their lifetimes. Now of women with that mutation, about half never will. There are other influences too, diet and exercise, hormone use, and today whether one gets a prophylactic mastectomy. So whether or not a woman will get cancer can't be predicted with certainty. However, we know that some women (with certain BrCa mutations) were born much more likely to get it. Moreover, while there are a myriad of things an individual woman can do to increase or decrease her risk over a lifetime, they can't choose to not get cancer.
